extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of communication and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes James W. Carey's 'ritual view' of communication and its contrast with the 'transmission view', including defining characteristics, examples (newspapers, Twitter), theoretical influences, and applied domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual view of communication — core definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication — the construction of a symbolic reality — represents, maintains, adapts, and shares the beliefs of a society in time; communication conceived as a process that enables and enacts societal transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carey defines the ritual view particularly in terms of sharing, participation, association, and fellowship; he also links it to commonness, communion, and community and highlights the term's religious connotations (ritual, ceremony) to emphasize shared beliefs. The ritual view embeds communication in cultural traditions and social relations rather than treating it as a mere transmission of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual view — characteristic: communal/horizontal process
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication in the ritual perspective is a more horizontal process within a community that binds the community together across time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ritual view treats communication as part of a broad cultural dialogue that reiterates preexisting traditions, often not fully conscious; it emphasizes shared participation and maintenance of community rather than centralized, one-way dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual view — characteristic terms (sharing, participation, association, fellowship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carey characterizes the ritual view in terms of sharing, participation, association, and fellowship (and relatedly commonness, communion, community).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms indicate modes of engagement (e.g., habitual newspaper reading, following on Twitter) through which symbolic reality is reproduced and affirmed over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission view of communication — core definition
rubrics_metrics.description: In the transmission view the dissemination of information constitutes the primary goal; defined in terms of imparting, sending, transmitting and giving information to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transmission view emphasizes the conscious role of agents seeking to influence an audience; it conceptualizes communication as a linear, causal process (e.g., Lasswell's 'who says what to whom through what channels with what effect') typically from centralized producers to distributed audiences, and often frames dissemination as a means of control (Carey cites ancient Egypt messaging/transportation example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission view — characteristic: vertical/agent-centered, control-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmission emphasizes power and control exercised by creators of messages over receivers, a vertical relationship from centralized media producers outward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses evaluation on sender intent, message effect, and distribution across space; contrasts with ritual view's focus on cultural maintenance and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical relation between ritual and transmission views
rubrics_metrics.description: The ritual/transmission dichotomy is an analytical distinction rather than an absolute opposition; neither view necessarily denies what the other affirms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carey advises using both perspectives to achieve a nuanced understanding of human interaction; researchers should not treat them as mutually exclusive when evaluating communication phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as an example of ritual communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper reading is likened to attending mass: a ritual where little new is learned but a particular view of the world is portrayed and confirmed; the act becomes part of shared culture and maintained through time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carey notes readers engage in shifts of roles/dramatic focus while habitually consuming news; evaluation of newspapers from a ritual perspective focuses on how they present and confirm a shared symbolic reality and sustain community ties (cf. Keith R. Stamm's work on newspaper use and community ties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital media and social media's effect on ritual communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Digitized newspapers and social media change immediacy, geography, and connectedness of news consumption, raising questions about how communities sustained by newspapers are transformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page highlights that social media (e.g., Twitter) can enable establishment, transformation, and maintenance of societal interaction through 'tweets' (sharing/participation) and 'following' (association/fellowship), forming online communities; analysts should consider platform-specific dynamics when applying the ritual view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter as an instance of ritualized online community formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter enables ritualized practices (following, tweeting) that create online communities where users share beliefs and form habitual patterns of consumption and interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article points to research (e.g., group polarization studies after George Tiller's death) showing users primarily interact with like-minded individuals, seeking affirmation of established beliefs and engaging antagonistically with dissidents — an example of ritual processes producing echo chambers and polarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of community in electric age/Internet — media shapes societal fabric
rubrics_metrics.description: The electric age (and Internet) redefined community on a global scale; community exists to the extent of shared beliefs rather than as a unified cohesive group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carey (drawing on Dewey, Innis, McLuhan) and followers argue media influences and maintains societal fabric over time; evaluators should attend to how media technologies dissolve or reshape ritual/transmission tensions and the symbolic production of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domains of application for the ritual theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Carey's ritual theory has been applied as a theoretical framework to family stories, undergraduate studies, business practices, computer technologies, criminal behaviour, theology, advertising, sociology, anthropology, and geography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list signals where researchers and practitioners can use the ritual/transmission distinction; when applying the theory, choose appropriate empirical domains and methods suited to the ritual emphasis (e.g., qualitative studies of shared practices) or transmission emphasis (e.g., effect/metrics studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic production of reality — analytic focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Carey's broader analytic focus is on the 'symbolic production of reality' — how humans, often unconsciously, produce and reproduce shared meanings as part of daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should seek awareness of these symbolic processes to better understand and potentially reshape common culture; this implies studying habitual practices, rituals, and the cultural meanings media circulates, not only information transfer.
